TeMFpy: a Python library for converting fermionic mean-field states into tensor networks

Simon H. Hille⋆\star, Attila Szabó†\dagger

Department of Physics, University of Zürich, Zürich, Switzerland

⋆\star simon.hille@physik.uzh.ch , †\dagger attila.szabo@physik.uzh.ch

Abstract

We introduce TeMFpy, a Python library for converting fermionic mean-field states to finite or infinite matrix product state (MPS) form. TeMFpy includes new, efficient, and easy-to-understand algorithms for both Slater determinants and Pfaffian states. Together with Gutzwiller projection, these also allow the user to build variational wave functions for various strongly correlated electron systems, such as quantum spin liquids. We present all implemented algorithms in detail and describe how they can be accessed through TeMFpy, including full example workflows. TeMFpy is built on top of TeNPy and, therefore, integrates seamlessly with existing MPS-based algorithms.

1 Introduction

Fermionic mean-field (or Gaussian [7]) states are a class of variational wave functions of central importance. All eigenstates of non-interacting fermionic Hamiltonians are Gaussian. As such, they form the starting point of such mean-field approaches as Hartree–Fock theory and the BCS theory of superconductivity, which often provide an excellent account of strongly interacting quantum systems as well. Furthermore, “dressing” mean-field states with, e.g., Gutzwiller and Jastrow factors gives rise to even more powerful variational ansätze, which are widely deployed in variational quantum Monte Carlo (VMC) [4]. Through parton constructions and Gutzwiller projection, fermionic mean-field states also form the basis of the most widely used variational ansätze for quantum spin liquids [4, 37, 38, 32].

Mean-field states are, however, a special class of wave function and cannot fully account for interaction-induced phenomena. A more general approach is offered by tensor networks, which can represent mean-field and interacting quantum states equally well, with an expressive power systematically improvable through the number of variational parameters. Matrix product states (MPS), designed for one-dimensional systems, are particularly useful on account of such powerful ground-state optimisation algorithms as the density matrix renormalisation group (DMRG) [33] and variational uniform MPS (VUMPS) [36].

Given the individual success of these two approaches, it is desirable to combine the two. In particular, DMRG and VUMPS are typically initialised with a random MPS, which leaves them prone to converging to local minima, which potentially display qualitatively different physics to the true ground state. (Dressed) mean-field states (from, e.g., Hartree–Fock theory or VMC) are a much closer starting point, stabilising and reducing the computational cost of MPS optimisation [18, 16]. By initialising with different ansätze, we may also compare different mean-field theories as approximate descriptions of the physical system [35]. Using mean-field states as initial guesses, however, requires efficient algorithms to convert fermionic mean-field wave functions to an MPS form.

Furthermore, MPS representations give ready access to such quantities as the entanglement spectrum and entropy, which are difficult to obtain from VMC but often carry detailed information of exotic physics, such as topological order and the associated edge physics [19, 28]. This is a particularly appealing prospect for Gutzwiller-projected mean-field states, which are common ansatz wave functions for quantum spin liquids [4, 37, 38, 32], fractional quantum Hall states [15, 23, 24], and other topological orders [21], as the Gutzwiller projection is a local operation, so it can easily be applied to real-space MPS representations of mean-field states.

As first noted in Ref. [27], Slater determinants can conveniently be converted to MPS form, since their Schmidt vectors are themselves Slater determinants [25, 9, 26] and so entries of the canonical MPS tensors are overlaps of Slater determinants, which can be computed efficiently. Since then, this idea has been expanded to Pfaffian (or Bogoliubov mean-field) states [17] and successfully used to study Gutzwiller-projected mean-field states [40] and as starting points to DMRG [18, 16, 35].

In this paper, we introduce a new open-source Python library called TeMFpy for efficiently converting fermionic mean-field states to MPS form. TeMFpy provides both an easy-to-use interface for the key functionality of representing Slater determinants and Pfaffian states as either finite or infinite MPS and a number of well-defined building blocks for advanced users to build new algorithms. It is built on top of TeNPy [12], so that the resulting MPS representations can be used directly for further calculations with, e.g., DMRG. We hope that TeMFpy will open up the power of combining mean-field, VMC, and tensor-network approaches to a wide community of users.

1.1 Outline

The core functionality, constructing finite MPS representations of fermionic mean-field states, specified through either a (Nambu) mean-field Hamiltonian or a (Nambu) correlation matrix, is described in Sec. 2. In particular, Section 2.1 provides an overview of the interface and a guide to basic usage.

We introduce our new algorithms for computing MPS tensor entries for Slater determinants and Pfaffian states in detail in Secs. 2.2 and 2.3, respectively. In both cases, we exploit the fact that the leading Schmidt vectors that we keep only differ in the occupation of a few “entangled” orbitals [22, 20], so their overlaps can be reduced to a determinant or a Pfaffian defined only on these orbitals. In a typical Schmidt decomposition, the �\chi leading Schmidt vectors can be captured through nent=O⁡(log⁡�)n_{\mathrm{ent}}=O(\log\chi) entangled orbitals, so a single MPS tensor entry can be computed in O⁡(nent3)=O⁡(log3⁡�)O(n_{\mathrm{ent}}^{3})=O(\log^{3}\chi), rather than O⁡(L3)O(L^{3}), time, a dramatic speedup.

Section 3 discusses TeMFpy’s functionality for computing infinite MPS, based on ideas outlined in Ref. [27]. We provide both a generic implementation able to convert any finite MPS into infinite ones, as well as specialised algorithms for mean-field states in Sec. 3.1, which bypass the need to construct finite MPS for large systems. Finally, we implement Gutzwiller projection schemes in Sec. 4.

1.2 Installing TeMFpy

TeMFpy is written in pure Python (the current version 0.3.3 requires at least Python 3.10 and TeNPy 1.1.0) and is largely platform-agnostic.11 1 Installing the dependency (needed for handling Pfaffian states) for Windows is, however, not trivial, see here for details. You can also bypass this issue using the Windows Subsystem for Linux. It is available from PyPI using the command

⬇
1 pip install --upgrade temfpy

We will also make it available on CondaForge soon. The development version is available at https://github.com/temfpy/temfpy, where we also welcome issue reports, suggestions, and code contributions. A detailed API reference, examples, and tutorials are available online at https://temfpy.github.io/temfpy.

2 Converting mean-field states to MPS

Writing any quantum state as an MPS (in canonical form) relies on computing its Schmidt decomposition,

| ⟩=∑���(i)​|L�(i)⟩⊗g|R�(i)⟩,\ket{\psi}=\sum_{\alpha}\lambda_{\alpha}^{(i)}\ket{L_{\alpha}^{(i)}}\otimes_{g}\ket{R_{\alpha}^{(i)}}, (1)

where ��(i)\lambda_{\alpha}^{(i)} are the Schmidt values across entanglement cut ii, while |L�(i)⟩\ket{L_{\alpha}^{(i)}} and |R�(i)⟩\ket{R_{\alpha}^{(i)}} are the corresponding Schmidt vectors defined on the sites left and right to the same cut.22 2 In this paper, we always deal with Hilbert spaces of fermions, so the standard tensor product is replaced by the fermionic (Z2\mdmathbb{Z}_{2} graded) one, ⊗g\otimes_{g} [8]. This distinction will be particularly important when we come to Pfaffian states. Now, the entries of the left-canonical MPS tensor for a given site are given by the overlaps of the left Schmidt vectors for the entanglement cuts on either side of it [33]:

A�​�ni=(⟨ni|⊗g⟨L�(i−1)|)​|L�(i)⟩,A^{n_{i}}_{\alpha\beta}=\left(\langle n_{i}|\otimes_{g}\langle L^{(i-1)}_{\alpha}|\right)\;|L^{(i)}_{\beta}\rangle, (2a)
while right-canonical tensors are given by overlaps of right Schmidt vectors:
B�​�ni=(⟨R�(i)|⊗g⟨ni|)​|R�(i−1)⟩.B^{n_{i}}_{\beta\alpha}=\left(\langle R^{(i)}_{\alpha}|\otimes_{g}\langle n_{i}|\right)\;|R^{(i-1)}_{\beta}\rangle. (2b)

For a generic state, Eq. (2) is impractical to use directly. However, the eigenstates of fermionic mean-field Hamiltonians [5] of the form

H=∑i​j[ti​jfi†fj+(�i​jfi†fj†+h.c.)]H=\sum_{ij}\left[t_{ij}f^{\dagger}_{i}f_{j}+(\Delta_{ij}f^{\dagger}_{i}f^{\dagger}_{j}+\mathrm{h.c.})\right] (3)

are fermionic Gaussian states [7], that is, Slater determinants (if there are no pairing terms �i​j\Delta_{ij}) or Pfaffian (i.e., Bogoliubov mean-field) states. The Schmidt vectors of such states are in turn also Slater determinants or Pfaffian states and the (generalised) orbitals that define them can be obtained from diagonalising their single-particle correlation matrices [25, 9, 26]. The entries of the MPS tensor (2) thus reduce to overlaps of fermionic Gaussian states, which can be computed efficiently as determinants or Pfaffians of the overlaps of individual orbitals.

Furthermore, as the leading Schmidt vectors only differ in the occupation of a few of these (generalised) orbitals [22, 20], we can apply linear-algebra manipulations to these determinants and Pfaffians to reduce the computational complexity of computing each MPS tensor from O⁡(�2​N3)O(\chi^{2}N^{3}) [27] to O⁡(N3+�2​log3​�)O(N^{3}+\chi^{2}\log^{3}\chi), where NN is the size of the system and �\chi is the bond dimension of the tensor. Our algorithms thus differ significantly from those of Ref. [22, 20], as we do not rely on introducing an array of virtual fermion degrees of freedom and effectively compress several intermediate steps in their approach into one. We describe our method in detail in Secs. 2.2.2 and 2.3.3.

Warning for finite bond dimension.

In the limit �→∞\chi\to\infty, our method is exact as the MPS tensors are built from the overlaps of the exact Schmidt vectors and none of the wave function has to be truncated. In this ideal case, the final MPS is normalised, i.e., ⟨MPS|MPS⟩=1.0\braket{\mathrm{MPS}|\mathrm{MPS}}=1.0. For finite bond dimensions, however, some of the wave function must be truncated at every entanglement cut. This both lowers the norm ⟨MPS|MPS⟩\braket{\mathrm{MPS}|\mathrm{MPS}} from 1.0 and makes the MPS tensors slightly noncanonical. This issue is particularly important for cylinder MPS simulations of two-dimensional systems, where truncation errors are substantial even for large bond dimensions. Truncation error estimates for each MPS tensor are printed during the MPS conversion if logging is turned on using . The overall conversion error can be estimated from the deviation of the norm of the resulting MPS from 1.0.

2.2 Slater determinants

2.2.1 Schmidt decomposition

Given the correlation matrix Ci​j:=⟨cj†​ci⟩C_{ij}:=\braket{c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}} for a Slater determinant, we start by diagonalizing the correlation matrix restricted to subsystem AA:

2.2.2 Fast overlap computation

Evaluating (2) thus requires us to compute the overlaps of Slater determinants. (The on-site degree of freedom can be included in the “bra” Slater determinant as an additional site-localised orbital [27].) It is well known that such overlaps are given by the determinant of the matrix of overlaps of the individual orbitals; evaluating these determinants independently would yield the whole MPS tensor in O⁡(�2​N3)O(\chi^{2}N^{3}) time [27], where �\chi is the bond dimension of the MPS.

TeMFpy improves on this scaling by noting that the overlaps of the “occupied” orbitals in (8) appear in all of these determinants, i.e., the determinants can be written in the following block structure:55 5 For the sake of simplicity, we follow the case of left Schmidt vectors in what follows. Right Schmidt vectors can be dealt with analogously.

𝒮\displaystyle\mathcal{S} =𝒟−𝒞​A−1​ℬ\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}-\mathcal{C}A^{-1}\mathcal{B} (11)

2.3 Pfaffian (Bogoliubov mean-field) states

2.3.1 How to specify Hamiltonians and correlation matrices

From the user’s point of view, the main complication of the Pfaffian case compared to Slater determinants is the appearance of anomalous correlations ⟨c​c⟩\braket{cc}, ⟨c†​c†⟩\braket{c^{\dagger}c^{\dagger}}, which need to be specified together with the number-conserving ones. There are a number of conventions one can choose to specify the overall Nambu Hamiltonians and correlation matrices, of which TeMFpy supports two:

Complex-fermion basis.

The “basis” of single-particle operators are the creation and annihilation operators ci†c_{i}^{\dagger} and cic_{i}, listed as the row vector (ci†,ci)(c_{i}^{\dagger},c_{i}). The Nambu Hamiltonian matrix HH is interpreted as H^=(ci†,ci)​H​(cj†,cj)†\hat{H}=(c_{i}^{\dagger},c_{i})\;H\;(c_{j}^{\dagger},c_{j})^{\dagger}, i.e., it is expected to contain the coefficients of

(ci†​cjci†​cj†ci​cjci​cj†)\begin{pmatrix}c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}&c_{i}^{\dagger}c_{j}^{\dagger}\\[2.0pt] c_{i}c_{j}&c_{i}c_{j}^{\dagger}\end{pmatrix}

in this layout, while the correlation matrix is given by [5]

C=𝟙−⟨(ci†,ci)†​(cj†,cj)⟩=(⟨cj†​ci⟩⟨cj​ci⟩⟨cj†​ci†⟩⟨cj​ci†⟩).C=\mathbbm{1}-\left\langle(c_{i}^{\dagger},c_{i})^{\dagger}\;(c_{j}^{\dagger},c_{j})\right\rangle=\begin{pmatrix}\langle c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}\rangle&\langle c_{j}c_{i}\rangle\\[2.0pt] \langle c_{j}^{\dagger}c_{i}^{\dagger}\rangle&\langle c_{j}c_{i}^{\dagger}\rangle\end{pmatrix}. (13)

In particular, TeMFpy expects that the matrices consist of 2×22\times 2 blocks containing the Hamiltonian terms or correlators for a given pair of sites, i.e., that contain the correlators (13) for sites ii and jj.

Majorana basis.

Instead of the complex-fermion operators c,c†c,c^{\dagger}, we may also introduce the Majorana operators

2n =(cn†+cn)/2,\displaystyle=(c^{\dagger}_{n}+c_{n})/\sqrt{2}, 2n+1 =i⁡(cn†−cn)/2\displaystyle=i(c^{\dagger}_{n}-c_{n})/\sqrt{2} (14)

to define Nambu Hamiltonians and correlation matrices. Note that the normalisation of (14) differs from the usual one by a factor of 2\sqrt{2}: This makes the transformation between the two bases unitary, so the eigenvalues of the correlation matrix [and thus formulas like (17)] remain unchanged, allowing us to use largely the same code in both cases.

Naturally, entries Hi​jH_{ij} of the Hamiltonian matrix are expected to be the coefficients of ij{}_{i}{}_{j}, while the correlation matrix is given by Ci​j=𝟙−⟨ij⟩=⟨ji⟩C_{ij}=\mathbbm{1}-\braket{{}_{i}{}_{j}}=\braket{{}_{j}{}_{i}}.

Specifying the basis in TeMFpy.

This is controlled by the argument , which can be to compute the complex-fermion correlation matrix of a Majorana Hamiltonian, or vice versa with . One can also specify or , which does not change the basis but checks Nambu symmetry in the appropriate basis. (If is not specified, the correlation matrix in the input basis is computed, with no checks.) In addition, helper functions are provided for converting matrices and eigenvectors between the two bases and for checking Nambu symmetry.

Internally, uses the Majorana basis to diagonalise the correlation matrix, as this makes it easier to ensure Nambu symmetric eigenvectors, see Sec. B.2. From there on, however, we use the complex-fermion basis, as quantities such as the parity of Bogoliubov vacua or the overlaps (23) are more naturally written in those terms.

2.3.2 Schmidt decomposition

Schmidt vectors.

2.3.3 Fast overlap computation

Eq. (2) gives the MPS tensor entries as overlaps of Pfaffian states; the physical site can be included on the “bra” side through an additional Bogoliubov operator \gamma, set to either cic_{i} or ci†c_{i}^{\dagger} so as to ensure that the vacuum states on the two sides have the same parity (cf. Section C.2). Therefore, we need an efficient way of evaluating overlaps of the form

O=⟨vacA|​a�k​…​a�1​b�1†​…​b�m†​|vacB⟩,O=\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}}b^{\dagger}_{\beta_{1}}\dots b^{\dagger}_{\beta_{m}}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{B}}, (20)

where the a�a_{\alpha} and b�b_{\beta} are two complete sets of Bogoliubov operators and |vacA⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{A}} and |vacB⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{B}} are the Pfaffian states annihilated by them. Let the two sets of operators be related to one another by

(b†,b)=(a†,a)​(UV∗VU∗)(b^{\dagger},b)=(a^{\dagger},a)\begin{pmatrix}U&V^{*}\\ V&U^{*}\end{pmatrix} (21)

and assume that UU is not singular: this means that |vacA,B⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{A,B}} have the same parity and their overlap is nonzero. Then we have [5, 31]

|vacB⟩=|detU|×exp⁡(12​M�​�​a�†​a�†)​|vacA⟩,\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{B}}=\sqrt{|\det U|}\times\exp\left(\frac{1}{2}M_{\alpha\beta}a_{\alpha}^{\dagger}a_{\beta}^{\dagger}\right)\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}, (22)

where M=(V​U−1)∗M=(VU^{-1})^{*} is antisymmetric; the normalisation follows from the Onishi formula [30]. We can then show (Appendix D) that the overlap (20) is given by

O=|detU|×pf⁡(NB​BNB​A−(NB​A)TNA​A),O=\sqrt{|\det U|}\times\pf\begin{pmatrix}N^{BB}&N^{BA}\\ -(N^{BA})^{\mathrm{T}}&N^{AA}\end{pmatrix}, (23a)
where
Ni​jA​A\displaystyle N^{AA}_{ij} =M�i​�j,\displaystyle=M_{\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j}}, Ni​jB​A\displaystyle N^{BA}_{ij} =[(U∗)−1]�m+1−i​�j,\displaystyle=\left[(U^{*})^{-1}\right]_{\beta_{m+1-i}\alpha_{j}}, Ni​jB​B\displaystyle N^{BB}_{ij} =[(U∗)−1​V]�m+1−i​�m+1−j.\displaystyle=[(U^{*})^{-1}V]_{\beta_{m+1-i}\beta_{m+1-j}}. (23b)

That is, each overlap is given by a Pfaffian the size of which is determined by the number of Bogoliubov excitations in the defining Schmidt vectors, which is capped by the O⁡(log⁡�)O(\log\chi) number of active generalised orbitals. Therefore, computing a full MPS tensor takes O⁡(N3+�2​log3​�)O(N^{3}+\chi^{2}\log^{3}\chi) time, just like the Slater-determinant case. In terms of asymptotic complexity, this matches the approach of Ref. [17]; however, instead of a full Bloch–Messiah decomposition, the most complex operations involved here are matrix inversions, which does reduce the CPU time cost of the algorithm. TeMFpy uses the library [39] to compute the Pfaffians in (23).

3 Infinite MPS for gapped systems

The ground states of gapped, translation-invariant systems can efficiently be represented using matrix product states with finite bond dimensions even in the thermodynamic limit [36]. Due to translation invariance, the tensors of such an infinite MPS repeat with the periodicity of the Hamiltonian, so the whole infinite system can be captured by MPS tensors for a single unit cell of length kk.

Naïvely, we could obtain such an iMPS representation by computing the ground state of a sufficiently large finite system and extracting kk consecutive tensors An,…,An+k−1A_{n},\dots,A_{n+k-1} near the middle. However, we have to account for the gauge redundancy of MPS: on any given entanglement cut, redefining the MPS tensors as Ai′=Ai​XA^{\prime}_{i}=A_{i}X, Ai+1′=X−1​Ai+1A^{\prime}_{i+1}=X^{-1}A_{i+1} leaves the wave function invariant [33]. Even in the limit of very long systems, these gauge choices on entanglement cuts nn and n+kn+k will generically be different, so contracting them directly would change the wave function, see Fig. 2(a).

To construct valid iMPS tensors, we need to fix this gauge freedom. We follow the approach outlined in Ref. [27], which effectively replaces the Schmidt vectors |L(L,n)⟩\ket{L^{(L,n)}} and |R(L,n+k)⟩\ket{R^{(L,n+k)}}, which form the environment of the extracted unit cell, with those of a system one unit cell shorter, |L(L−k,n)⟩\ket{L^{(L-k,n)}} and |R(L−k,n)⟩\ket{R^{(L-k,n)}}: The latter are defined on the same entanglement cut, so their gauge degrees of freedom are necessarily consistent. The unitary rotations between these bases are given by

(C0)�​�\displaystyle(C_{0})_{\alpha\beta} =⟨L�(L−k,n)|L�(L,n)⟩,\displaystyle=\braket{L_{\alpha}^{(L-k,n)}|L_{\beta}^{(L,n)}}, (D0)�​�\displaystyle(D_{0})_{\alpha\beta} =⟨R�(L−k,n)|R�(L,n+k)⟩.\displaystyle=\braket{R_{\beta}^{(L-k,n)}|R_{\alpha}^{(L,n+k)}}. (24)

As illustrated in Fig. 2(b), replacing the first and last tensors in the unit cell, AnA_{n} and An+k−1A_{n+k-1}, with C0​AnC_{0}A_{n} and An+k−1​D0A_{n+k-1}D_{0} fixes the gauge on both ends of the unit cell to that of entanglement cut nn of the shorter chain. As such, the unit cell can now be repeated indefinitely without deforming the wave function, i.e., it is a valid iMPS unit cell. [For finite bond dimensions, the matrices C0,D0C_{0},D_{0} defined in (24) are only approximately unitary: we deal with this issue in Appendix E.]

The algorithm outlined above is implemented in the module for generic MPS, see Listing 2 for an example workflow.

3.1 Implementation for mean-field states

For Slater determinants and Pfaffian states, however, it is not necessary to construct the Schmidt states surrounding the iMPS unit cell as MPS, as their overlaps (24) can efficiently be computed the same way as MPS tensor entries, cf. Secs. 2.2.2 and 2.3.3. The classes and are able to compute such overlaps too.

and thus compute the MPS tensors of the longer chain for a single unit cell of the iMPS only, as well as the left and right Schmidt vectors for the reference entanglement cut nn of the shorter chain. The unitary rotation CC on the left end of the iMPS unit cell is applied the same way as explained above and in Appendix E for a generic MPS. By contrast, as we compute right canonical iMPS tensors, the unitary rotation at the right end can be combined into the construction of the last tensor by using the Schmidt vectors of the shorter chain [27]:

B~�​�nk\displaystyle\tilde{B}^{n_{k}}_{\alpha\beta} =B�​ nk(D0) ​�=⟨R�(L−k,n)|R(L,n+k)⟩×(⟨R(L,n+k)|⊗g⟨nk|)|R�(L,n+k−1)⟩\displaystyle=B^{n_{k}}_{\alpha\gamma}(D_{0})_{\gamma\beta}=\braket{R_{\beta}^{(L-k,n)}|R^{(L,n+k)}}\times\left(\langle R^{(L,n+k)}|\otimes_{g}\langle n_{k}|\right)\,|R^{(L,n+k-1)}_{\alpha}\rangle
=(⟨R�(L−k,n)|⊗g⟨nk|)​|R�(L,n+k−1)⟩,\displaystyle=\left(\langle R^{(L-k,n)}_{\beta}|\otimes_{g}\langle n_{k}|\right)\,|R^{(L,n+k-1)}_{\alpha}\rangle, (25)

(summation over Greek Schmidt-vector indices implied) because the Schmidt vectors |R(L,n+k)⟩\ket{R^{(L,n+k)}} form a complete orthonormal basis. As such, these routines do not return any estimate of the conversion error introduced on the right end of the iMPS unit cell.

Furthermore, it avoids the truncation errors introduced by converting the environments of the iMPS unit cell to MPS form (cf. the error estimates in Listings 2 and 3).

4 Gutzwiller projection

In addition to studying them directly or using them as starting points for DMRG on fermionic systems, mean-field wave functions are also useful building blocks for studying such exotic systems as quantum spin liquids or fractional quantum Hall states [4, 37, 38, 32, 15, 23, 24, 21]. These are often described by parton constructions, where the physical degrees of freedom are split up into a number of fractionalised quasiparticles, which capture the physics of the strongly entangled phase already at mean-field level. This construction, however, enlarges the Hilbert space on each lattice site: To recover a wave function of the original system, the additional degrees of freedom must be removed by acting with a Gutzwiller projection operator on every site. This is quite a natural operation for matrix product states, as the Gutzwiller projector can be applied directly to the physical leg(s) associated with each site, resulting in a (generally no longer canonical) MPS with unchanged virtual space.

There are many Gutzwiller projection schemes, appropriate for different parton constructions. As an illustration of the general principle, we implemented Gutzwiller projection for quantum spin liquids in spin-1/21/2 systems, which are often described using mean-field theories of Abrikosov fermions:

S→i\displaystyle\vec{S}_{i} =12​fi​�†​�→�​�​fi​�,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}f^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}\vec{\sigma}\!_{\alpha\beta}f_{i\beta}, (fi​�†​fi​�CLOSE\displaystyle(f^{\dagger}_{i\alpha}f_{i\alpha} OPEN=1)\displaystyle=1) (26)

where �→\vec{\sigma} are the Pauli matrices and Greek indices (summation implied) stand for the Abrikosov-fermion species ↑,↓\uparrow,\downarrow. The on-site Hilbert space of the Abrikosov fermions is four-dimensional, which is reduced to the spin-1/21/2 Hilbert space by imposing single occupancy on each site. We implement this projection scheme in . The input MPS is expected to have 2​L2L spinless fermion sites: sites 2​i2i and 2​i+12i+1 represent modes fi↑f_{i\uparrow} and fi↓f_{i\downarrow}, respectively. The function groups these pairs of sites, projects out the unphysical (empty/doubly occupied) sector of each on-site Hilbert space, and reinterprets the remaining two-dimensional Hilbert space as a spin-1/21/2 degree of freedom. Since the only conserved quantum number of the input MPS is (the parity of the) fermion number, which is fixed by the projection, the output spin MPS will not carry any symmetry quantum numbers.

Spin liquids in Heisenberg models, however, preserve spin-rotation symmetry, which implies that the Abrikosov-fermion mean-field theories that describe them may only contain singlet hopping and pairing terms [37, 3, 2]. Similar to singlet superconductivity [4], these terms can all be treated as hopping if we perform a particle–hole transformation on one spin species:

ci,↑\displaystyle c_{i,\uparrow} :=fi,↑,\displaystyle:=f_{i,\uparrow}, ci,↓\displaystyle c_{i,\downarrow} :=fi,↓†.\displaystyle:=f_{i,\downarrow}^{\dagger}. (27)

In terms of the cc operators, the valid spin Hilbert space corresponds to empty (spin down) and fully occupied (spin up) sites.77 7 We also note that the full gauge freedom of spin liquids is most naturally expressed in terms of mixing the cc particles [1, 37]. This Gutzwiller projection is implemented in
, whose input sites are expected to correspond to the fermionic modes ci↑c_{i\uparrow} and ci↓c_{i\downarrow}. Since in this convention, the fermion occupation number corresponds to magnetisation along the �z\sigma^{z} axis, number-conserving (Slater-determinant) states are projected to U⁡(1)U(1) spin-preserving MPS.

U⁡(1)U(1) quantum spin liquids can be represented using mean-field Hamiltonians containing only spin-independent hopping terms, HMF=∑i​j​�ti​j​fi​�†​fj​�H_{\mathrm{MF}}=\sum_{ij\sigma}t_{ij}f_{i\sigma}^{\dagger}f_{j\sigma} [37, 38, 32]. The correlation matrices of such states consist of decoupled spin-up and spin-down blocks that are either equal (in the ff convention) or related by C↑=𝟙−C↓C_{\uparrow}=\mathbbm{1}-C_{\downarrow} (in the cc convention). For convenience, we provide the function that turns the correlation matrix for a single spin species into such an enlarged correlation matrix, compatible with either convention. This function can also be applied to the input correlation matrix by passing the argument (ff convention) or (cc convention) to etc.

An illustration of this functionality is given in Listing 4. We have not tried to build a catalogue of all useful Gutzwiller projection schemes with this first release. However, we welcome and look forward to users who deploy TeMFpy to other strongly correlated systems enriching the library by contributing their Gutzwiller projection schemes.

5 Example workflow: Gutzwiller-projected wave functions and flux threading for the kagome Heisenberg model

The most promising candidate for the ground state of the antiferromagnetic spin-1/2 Heisenberg model

H^=J​∑⟨i​j⟩𝐒^i⋅𝐒^j\hat{H}=J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{i}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{S}}_{j} (28)

on the kagome lattice is a gapless U⁡(1)U(1) Dirac spin liquid (DSL) [11, 29, 14, 13]. As an illustrative example for a typical workflow with TeMFpy, we consider the following hopping-only parton ansatz for the DSL:

H^�−flux=−∑�=↑,↓∑<i​j>ei​'i​jf†i,�fj,�≡∑�​�f†�h�​�f�,\hat{H}_{\pi-\mathrm{flux}}=-\sum_{\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow}\sum_{<ij>}e^{i\varphi_{ij}}f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f_{j,\sigma}\equiv\sum_{\alpha\beta}f^{\dagger}_{\alpha}h_{\alpha\beta}f_{\beta}, (29)

where the fi,�f_{i,\sigma} are a pair of Abrikosov fermions on site ii, Greek indices stand for the combination of site and spin species, and the phases 'i​j\varphi_{ij} are chosen such that the total flux for a parton traversing a hexagon (triangle) is �\pi (0). Implementing this flux pattern requires extending the unit cell to six sites; we use the phase pattern shown in Fig. 3(a). The resulting band structure has two Dirac cones per spin species [Fig. 3(b)].

5.1 Spin-flux threading

Ref. [13] identified Dirac cones in the spin model (28) using spin-flux threading, that is, by inserting a spin rotation by angle �\theta into the periodic boundary conditions around the cylinder:

Sx,y,s±\displaystyle S^{\pm}_{x,y,s} =e±i​�​Sx+�,y+L2,s±;\displaystyle=e^{\pm i\theta}S^{\pm}_{x+\Delta,y+L_{2},s}; Sx,y,sz\displaystyle S^{z}_{x,y,s} =Sx+�,y+L2,sz,\displaystyle=S^{z}_{x+\Delta,y+L_{2},s}, (30)

where sites are indexed with the position x,yx,y of the containing 6-site unit cell in units of the lattice vectors a→1,2\vec{a}_{1,2} [Fig. 3(a)], and the index 0≤s<60\leq s<6 of the site within the unit cell, and L2L_{2} is the number of 6-site unit cells around the cylinder. The periodicity of the cylinder does not have to line up with the lattice direction a→2\vec{a}_{2}; rather, winding around the cylinder may move the particle along the a→1\vec{a}_{1} direction by �\Delta unit cells. In particular, we will use L2=2L_{2}=2 and �=1\Delta=1 [13]: The latter means that consecutive six-site unit cells form a spiral on which each unit cell is surrounded by identical environments, that is, we can use an iMPS unit cell of 6 sites regardless of L2L_{2}. Furthermore, we can split the spin rotation (30) uniformly between the L2L_{2} unit cells by deforming the Heisenberg Hamiltonian as

H^(�)=J∑⟨i​j⟩(S^izS^jz+12[S^i+S^j−e�​[cell⁡(i)−cell⁡(j)]/L2+h.c.]),\hat{H}(\theta)=J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}\left(\hat{S}_{i}^{z}\hat{S}_{j}^{z}+\frac{1}{2}\left[\hat{S}_{i}^{+}\hat{S}_{j}^{-}e^{\theta[\mathrm{cell}(i)-\mathrm{cell}(j)]/L_{2}}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right]\right), (31)

where cell⁡(i)\mathrm{cell}(i) stands for the index of the unit cell containing site ii in the spiral. Writing (31) in terms of Abrikosov fermions and performing the same mean-field decoupling that generates (29) in the untwisted case yields

H^�−flux(�)=−∑�∑<i​j>ei​'i​jfi,�†fj,�e�​�​[cell⁡(i)−cell⁡(j)]/2​L2,\hat{H}_{\pi-\mathrm{flux}}(\theta)=-\sum_{\sigma}\sum_{<ij>}e^{i\varphi_{ij}}f^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}f_{j,\sigma}e^{\sigma\theta[\mathrm{cell}(i)-\mathrm{cell}(j)]/2L_{2}}, (32)

where �=↑,↓\sigma=\uparrow,\downarrow stand for +1,−1+1,-1 in the exponential [13]. In other words, the effective Hamiltonians of up- (down-)spin partons acquire flux �/2\theta/2 (−�/2-\theta/2) for winding around the cylinder.

The eigenstates of a single-particle Hamiltonian on the cylinder are the same as those on the open plane, provided the wave function is compatible with the periodic boundary conditions. This requirement selects lines in kk-space parallel to the length of the cylinder; adding a phase twist to the boundary conditions shifts the lines of allowed momenta around the cylinder [Fig. 3(b)]. In particular, for our geometry, the lines of allowed momenta pass through the Dirac cones of the �\pi-flux Hamiltonian (29) for �=�\theta=\pi. At this point, correlations become algebraic even on the finite-width cylinder; due to the Dirac dispersion of excitations, the correlation length should diverge as �−1∼|�−�|\xi^{-1}\sim|\theta-\pi|. This inverse correlation length can be extracted from an iMPS transfer matrix as the logarithm of its leading eigenvalue, �−1=log⁡�\xi^{-1}=\log\lambda [33, 13].

5.2 The TeMFpy workflow

Building the mean-field Hamiltonian.

The TeMFpy workflow starts by writing out the quadratic fermion Hamiltonian h�​�h_{\alpha\beta} as an explicit matrix. For an iMPS representation in particular, we need this Hamiltonian for two cylinders whose lengths differ by the desired iMPS unit cell and which are long enough for the iMPS unit cell extracted from the middle of the cylinder to be representative of the thermodynamic limit. Since the Hamiltonian is block diagonal in spin space and h↓​(�)=(h↑​(�))∗h_{\downarrow}(\theta)=\bigl(h_{\uparrow}(\theta)\bigr)^{*}, we only need to construct h↑​(�)h_{\uparrow}(\theta):88 8 For the sake of readability, we omit the construction of the Hamiltonian here. The unabridged example can be found in the online documentation.

We start this step by computing the correlation matrix of h↑​(�)h_{\uparrow}(\theta) at half-filling using . Next, we need to expand this to a correlation matrix for partons of both spin; as explained in Sec. 4, we also perform a particle-hole rotation on the down spins so that the U⁡(1)U(1) particle number correspond to SzS^{z}. 12 return C
13
14 C_short_spinful = spinful_C_with_conjugation(H_short_spinless)
15 C_long_spinful = spinful_C_with_conjugation(H_long_spinless)

Note that the up- and down-spin Abrikosov fermions on each site must be next to one another in the MPS to make Gutzwiller projection possible.

Mean-field and Gutzwiller-projected iMPS.

We now reach the main functionality of TeMFpy, the conversion of mean-field states to MPS form. As explained in Sec. 3, we have to specify which unit cell of the longer mean-field state should be extracted as a representative of the thermodynamic limit. This unit cell should align with the repeating unit cell of the mean-field Hamiltonian (in our case, it should start and end at integer multiples of the 2×6=122\times 6=12-site unit cell) and be as close to the centre of the longer cylinder as possible:

⬇
1 from temfpy.slater import C_to_iMPS
2 from temfpy.gutzwiller import abrikosov_ph
3
4 cut = 12 ∗ ((L1 ∗ L2 - 1) // 2) # Start of middle unit cell in C_short
5 psi_parton, err = C_to_iMPS(
6 C_short = C_short_spinful,
7 C_long = C_long_spinful,
8 trunc_par = {’chi_max’: 2000},
9 sites_per_cell = 12, # size of iMPS unit cell to extract
10 cut = cut,
11 )
12
13 # Gutzwiller projection
14 # Creates new MPS object by default; consume input MPS with inplace=True
15 # Converts to canonical form by default; disable with return_canonical=False
16 psi_spin = abrikosov_ph(psi_parton, inplace=False, return_canonical=True)

A high bond dimension should be used for constructing the mean-field state, since the full fermionic state contains more degrees of freedom and is hence more entangled than the spin state left behind after Gutzwiller projection.

Correlation-length spectra.

As explained above, we now look for Dirac-cone signatures in the �\theta-dependence of the correlation lengths associated with the parton-parton correlator ⟨ci↑†​cj↑⟩\langle c_{i\uparrow}^{\dagger}c_{j\uparrow}\rangle in the mean-field Hamiltonian H↑H_{\uparrow} [Fig. 4(a)] as well as the spin-spin correlator ⟨Si+​Sj−⟩\langle S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{-}\rangle in the Gutzwiller-projected DSL state [Fig. 4(b)]. Since these operators change the conserved quantum numbers of the iMPS (particle number and 2​Sz2S^{z}, respectively), the relevant eigenvalues of the iMPS transfer matrix are those associated with eigenvectors of the appropriate nonzero charge (1 and 2, respectively). For example, the spin-spin correlation lengths are obtained as follows:

⬇
1 from tenpy.networks import TransferMatrix
2
3 tm = TransferMatrix(psi_spin, psi_spin, charge_sector=[2])
4 num_ev = 20
5 eigV, _ = tm.eigenvectors(num_ev = num_ev)
6 inverse_correlation_length = -np.log(np.abs(eigV))

The overall structure of both spectra agrees with the iDMRG results of [13]. However, a qualitative difference appears near �=�\theta=\pi: The spectrum of correlation lengths is asymmetrical around this point, with inverse correlation lengths going well below those found with DMRG for |�|>�|\theta|>\pi. We attribute this to the different geometries underlying the iMPS construction in the two methods: While iDMRG works directly in the thermodynamic limit, TeMFpy extracts the iMPS unit cell from the bulk of a finite cylinder, which has (non-topological) edge modes in its single-particle spectrum. These give rise to a wide, nearly gapless region at |�|¦�|\theta|\gtrsim\pi, see Fig. 4(c).

Gutzwiller-boosted iDMRG.

The iMPS generated with TeMFpy can also serve as an initial state for iDMRG. Previous studies [18] have shown that mean-field initial states can improve convergence and help avoid local minima in finite-size DMRG. For iDMRG on the kagome Heisenberg model, however, the SzS^{z} product state trivial=|↑↓↑↓↑↓⟩{}_{\mathrm{trivial}}=\ket{\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow\uparrow\downarrow} and the Gutzwiller-projected �\pi-flux ansatz converge to the same ground-state energy [Fig. 4(d)]. The latter starts from a significantly lower initial energy, confirming the parton model (29) as a good candidate description of the true ground state; however, the cost of computing the initial iMPS environment for a state with a high bond dimension (note the very long runtime of the first iDMRG iteration) outweighs this benefit for iDMRG. We note, however, that this behaviour is model-dependent: In particular, it is much harder to write down good fermionic trial states, making the ability to convert Hartree–Fock states to MPS form particularly useful for strongly-correlated-electron systems.

6 Conclusion

We have presented TeMFpy, a Python library for converting fermionic mean-field states to MPS form. The library incorporates functionality for both Slater determinants and Pfaffian states, as well as finite and infinite MPS representations. We have aimed to make the key functionality readily accessible to users without understanding the details of the algorithm. Nevertheless, the library is fully modular, allowing users to easily prototype new applications of our algorithms. While the algorithms we use are not entirely new [27, 17, 22, 20], we have devised and incorporated several improvements that make the calculations both more efficient and numerically stable. Equally importantly, an easy-to-use open-source implementation of these algorithms, based around an existing tensor-network library [12], opens up its potential to a wide range of potential users.

In the future, we will improve and expand the capabilities of TeMFpy, while maintaining a clean, user-friendly, and backwards-compatible interface. A particularly interesting prospect is incorporating the approach of [22] adapted to bosonic Gaussian states, where our linear-algebra manipulations fail, but by introducing virtual boson degrees of freedom, the problem might still be reduced to computing permanents of a manageable size. Furthermore, we will expand the Gutzwiller-projection facility in to a wider range of parton constructions. In particular, we plan to design a general interface that allows users to prototype the projection schemes relevant to their work without a detailed understanding of TeNPy. In addition to TeNPy, we would like to support generating MPS in formats suitable for other tensor-network libraries, such as ITensor [10]. Last but not least, we will also expand the worked examples published with the codebase in order to illustrate more workflows and to help users get started with similar projects.

In all of this, we are looking forward to the support of the community of users, which we hope will build up around TeMFpy, as it will be deployed for studying (Gutzwiller-projected) mean-field states, seeding DMRG/VUMPS, and other applications we do not yet anticipate.

Complexity.

If only the �\chi subsets with the lowest sums are required, the inner loop of Algorithm 1 can clearly be terminated at step i=�i=\chi instead of running to 2n2^{n}. Appendix B Mutual diagonalisation of CL​LC^{LL}, CL​RC^{LR}, and CR​RC^{RR}

The correlation matrices of both Slater determinants and Pfaffian states must satisfy C2=CC^{2}=C [5]: Intuitively, all eigenvalues of CC must be either 1 (corresponding to filled orbitals or Bogoliubov operators that annihilate the Pfaffian) or 0 (corresponding to empty orbitals or Bogoliubov excitations). This also implies that the eigenvalues of the diagonal submatrices of CC are between 0 and 1.

Upon introducing an entanglement cut that splits the system into a left (LL) and a right (RR) half, it is natural to split the correlation matrix into blocks:

C=(CL​LCL​R(CL​R)†CR​R)C=\begin{pmatrix}C^{LL}&C^{LR}\\ (C^{LR})^{\dagger}&C^{RR}\end{pmatrix} (B.1)

(note that CC is Hermitian by definition), for which C2=CC^{2}=C implies

(CL​L)2+CL​R​(CL​R)†\displaystyle(C^{LL})^{2}+C^{LR}(C^{LR})^{\dagger} =CL​L\displaystyle=C^{LL} (B.2a)
CL​L​CL​R+CL​R​CR​R\displaystyle C^{LL}C^{LR}+C^{LR}C^{RR} =CL​R\displaystyle=C^{LR} (B.2b)
(CL​R)†​CL​R+(CR​R)2\displaystyle(C^{LR})^{\dagger}C^{LR}+(C^{RR})^{2} =CR​R;\displaystyle=C^{RR}; (B.2c)

as CC is Hermitian, the (CL​R)†(C^{LR})^{\dagger} block does not yield an independent constraint.

Let uu be an eigenvector of CL​LC^{LL} with eigenvalue �\lambda. Then by (B.2a), uu is also an eigenvector of CL​R​(CL​R)†C^{LR}(C^{LR})^{\dagger} with eigenvalue �​(1−�)\lambda(1-\lambda), i.e., it is a left singular vector of CL​RC^{LR} with singular value �=�​(1−�)\sigma=\sqrt{\lambda(1-\lambda)}. Likewise, (B.2c) implies that every eigenvector of CR​RC^{RR} is a right singular vector of CL​RC^{LR}.

Let now 0<�<10<\lambda<1, i.e., let uu define an entangled orbital. Then the normalised right singular vector corresponding to uu is

v\displaystyle v =(CL​R)†​u�\displaystyle=\frac{(C^{LR})^{\dagger}u}{\sigma} u\displaystyle u =CL​R​v�.\displaystyle=\frac{C^{LR}v}{\sigma}. (B.3)

Now, multiplying (B.2b)† from the right by u/�u/\sigma yields

(CL​R)†​CL​L​u�+CR​R​v\displaystyle\frac{(C^{LR})^{\dagger}C^{LL}u}{\sigma}+C^{RR}v =v\displaystyle=v
CR​R​v\displaystyle C^{RR}v =(1−�)​v.\displaystyle=(1-\lambda)v. (B.4)

That is, the eigenvalues of CL​LC^{LL} and CR​RC^{RR} corresponding to matching left and right singular vectors of CL​RC^{LR} sum to 1.

Finally, noting that the eigenbases of CL​LC^{LL} and CR​RC^{RR} provide a full complement of left and right singular vectors of CL​RC^{LR} and that �≠0\sigma\neq 0 only for the entangled modes 0<�<10<\lambda<1, we have the following singular-value decomposition of CL​RC^{LR}:

CL​R=∑ent�​(1−�)​u�​v1−�†,\displaystyle C^{LR}=\sum_{\mathrm{ent}}\sqrt{\lambda(1-\lambda)}\;u_{\lambda}\,v_{1-\lambda}^{\dagger}, (B.5)

where the subscripts indicate the eigenvalues corresponding to each eigenvector, and uu and vv are related by (B.3).

B.1 Implementation for Slater determinants

In case both left and right Schmidt vectors are needed for a single entanglement cut, the phase relation (B.3) between the entangled eigenvectors of CL​LC_{LL} and CR​RC_{RR} must be fixed in addition to diagonalising them.

Suppose that the columns of the matrix U~\tilde{U} contain the eigenvectors of CL​LC^{LL} with eigenvalue �\lambda, while V~\tilde{V} contains the eigenvectors of CR​RC^{RR} with eigenvalue 1−�1-\lambda. Then (B.2) implies

C~L​R:=U~†​CL​R​V~=�​(1−�)​W,\tilde{C}^{LR}:=\tilde{U}^{\dagger}C^{LR}\tilde{V}=\sigma(1-\sigma)W, (B.6)

where WW is an arbitrary unitary matrix. We fix this unitary degree of freedom by an additional SVD within the degenerate block:

C~L​R\displaystyle\tilde{C}^{LR} =P​�​Q†⟹\displaystyle=P\Sigma Q^{\dagger}\implies U\displaystyle U :=U~​P\displaystyle:=\tilde{U}P V\displaystyle V :=V~​Q.\displaystyle:=\tilde{V}Q. (B.7)

UU and VV are still eigenvectors of CL​LC^{LL} and CR​RC^{RR} with respective eigenvalues �\lambda and 1−�1-\lambda, but in addition, they are also matching singular vectors of CL​RC^{LR}. Doing this for all degenerate blocks, we obtain all corresponding pairs of entangled Schmidt modes. To make the best use of vectorisation in NumPy, we group the degenerate subspaces by multiplicity, so that all matrices U,V,C~L​R,…U,V,\tilde{C}^{LR},\dots of the same size may be handled together.

B.2 Implementation for Pfaffian states

Degenerate eigenspaces of CL​LC^{LL} and CR​RC^{RR} are handled largely the same way for Pfaffian states. Maintaining the Nambu symmetry (16), however, requires two modifications:

  • •

    Generically, the numerical diagonalisation of CL​LC^{LL} and CR​RC^{RR} does not return eigenvectors that respect (16). Therefore, we perform the gauge fixing (B.7) only for eigenspaces U~:=NL,ent,�\tilde{U}:=N_{L,\mathrm{ent},\lambda} and V~:=NR,ent,1−�\tilde{V}:=N_{R,\mathrm{ent},1-\lambda} with �<1/2\lambda<1/2. (This latter is also done for the non-entangled modes.)

  • •

    For �=1/2\lambda=1/2, the Nambu-partner eigenvectors are degenerate. In this case, it is convenient to work in the Majorana basis, where these pairs of eigenvectors are simply complex conjugates of one another: This implies that their real and imaginary parts are also eigenvectors and orthogonal to one another.

    That is, the �=1/2\lambda=1/2 eigenspace (of dimension dd) has a complete real basis. Numerically, we obtain this by an SVD of the concatenated real and imaginary parts of the generically complex eigenvectors: To numerical accuracy, dd of the singular values is 1, corresponding to the real eigenvectors r�r_{\alpha}; the remaining dd singular values are 0.

    In the Majorana basis, CL​RC^{LR} is purely imaginary, so rL†​Im⁡(CL​R)​rRr_{L}^{\dagger}\Im(C^{LR})r_{R} has a purely real SVD, which can be used to transform rL,rRr_{L},r_{R} so that rL†​CL​R​rR=i/2×𝟙dr_{L}^{\dagger}C^{LR}r_{R}=i/2\times\mathbbm{1}_{d}. From these, finally, orthonormal and Nambu-symmetric eigenvectors of CL​LC^{LL} and CL​RC^{LR} satisfying (18) can be obtained as

Appendix C Handling fermion anticommutation

C.1 Slater determinants

Expanding (8).

For a proper Schmidt decomposition we need to multiply (8) out, taking care of the fermionic anticommutation signs. A typical term takes the form

|S⟩\displaystyle\ket{S} =∏�∈OLdL,�†​(…​dR,i+1†​dL,i†​dR,i−1†​…)​∏�∈ORdR,�†​|vac⟩\displaystyle=\prod_{\mu\in O_{L}}d^{\dagger}_{L,\mu}\left(\dots d^{\dagger}_{R,i+1}d^{\dagger}_{L,i}d^{\dagger}_{R,i-1}\dots\right)\prod_{\nu\in O_{R}}d^{\dagger}_{R,\nu}\ket{\mathrm{vac}} (C.1)
=sgn⁡(�)​[∏�∈OLdL,�†​(…​dL,i†​…)​|vacL⟩]⊗g[(…​dR,i−1†​dR,i+1†​…)​∏�∈ORdR,�†​|vacR⟩],\displaystyle=\mathrm{sgn(\pi)}\left[\prod_{\mu\in O_{L}}d^{\dagger}_{L,\mu}\left(\dots d^{\dagger}_{L,i}\dots\right)\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{L}}\right]\otimes_{g}\left[\left(\dots d^{\dagger}_{R,i-1}d^{\dagger}_{R,i+1}\dots\right)\prod_{\nu\in O_{R}}d^{\dagger}_{R,\nu}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{R}}\right], (C.2)

where �\pi is the permutation that permutes all entangled operators dR†d^{\dagger}_{R} through the entangled operators dL†d^{\dagger}_{L} and reverses their order.

One can build �\pi by moving the right entangled orbitals one by one to the right. Due to their reversed order, the number of swaps needed for each orbital depends only on its initial position ii in the list of entangled orbitals, where the indexing starts from 0 on the right, see Fig. 5. To account for the resulting anticommutation signs, we multiply each entangled orbital operator dR,i†d^{\dagger}_{R,i} by (−1)i(-1)^{i}.

Reclassification of entangled orbitals.

If the bond dimension is limited to �\chi, some entangled orbitals may in fact be occupied in every Schmidt vector we keep. To be able to include them in the submatrix AA in (10), these need to be commuted through the remaining entangled orbitals, introducing an anticommutation sign. It is useful to view this as commuting all remaining entangled orbitals one by one through the newly classified ones. The anticommutation sign incurred in each of these steps depends only on the number of occupied orbital operators it needs to be commuted through, see Fig. 6: We account for these signs by multiplying them to the corresponding orbital eigenvectors.

C.2 Pfaffian states

Expanding (19).

For a proper Schmidt decomposition, we need to multiply (19) out, taking care of the fermionic anticommutation signs. A typical term takes the form

|S⟩=L,�1†R,�1†…L,�k†R,�k†|vacL⟩⊗g|vacR⟩\displaystyle\ket{S}={}_{L,\alpha_{1}}^{\dagger}{}_{R,\alpha_{1}}^{\dagger}\dots{}_{L,\alpha_{k}}^{\dagger}{}_{R,\alpha_{k}}^{\dagger}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{L}}\otimes_{g}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{R}} =L,�1†…L,�k†R,�k†…R,�1†|vacL⟩⊗g|vacR⟩,\displaystyle={}_{L,\alpha_{1}}^{\dagger}\dots{}_{L,\alpha_{k}}^{\dagger}{}_{R,\alpha_{k}}^{\dagger}\dots{}_{R,\alpha_{1}}^{\dagger}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{L}}\otimes_{g}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{R}}, (C.3)

which differs from (1) in that the operators and states of the left- and right-half Hilbert spaces are not separated from one another. That is, we need to commute the kk †R{}_{R}^{\dagger} operators across |vacL⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{L}}. If the latter is parity odd, each of these steps incur a negative sign [8], so we end up with

|S⟩=(−1)k​�L​(…L,�1†​|vacL⟩L,�k†)⊗g(…R,�k†​|vacR⟩R,�1),\displaystyle\ket{S}=(-1)^{k\pi_{L}}\left({}_{L,\alpha_{1}}^{\dagger}\dots{}_{L,\alpha_{k}}^{\dagger}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{L}}\right)\otimes_{g}\left({}_{R,\alpha_{k}}^{\dagger}\dots{}_{R,\alpha_{1}}\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{R}}\right), (C.4)

where �L=0,1\pi_{L}=0,1 is the parity of |vacL⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{L}}, computed using the Bloch–Messiah decomposition [6]. To account for this additional fermionic sign in the TeMFpy implementation, we

  • •

    list the † operators in the definition of left and right Schmidt states in opposite order (namely, in the code, we list them in increasing order of ��\lambda_{\alpha} on the left and in decreasing order on the right);

  • •

    and flip the sign of all R,R†{}_{R},{}_{R}^{\dagger} operators if the Bogoliubov vacuum |vacL⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{L}} is parity odd.

Parity matching for Pfaffian overlaps.

The Pfaffian overlap formula (23) is only valid if the vacua |vacA⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{A}} and |vacB⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{B}} have the same fermion parity, which is not necessarily the case for Schmidt states on different entanglement cuts. We remedy this problem by particle-hole transforming one Bogoliubov operator a0a_{0} on the bra side: a0↔a0†a_{0}\leftrightarrow a_{0}^{\dagger}, ⟨vacA′|:=⟨vacA|​a0\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}^{\prime}}:=\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{0}. For numerical stability, we choose the most entangled (i.e., �\lambda closest to 1/21/2, or the on-site mode for MPS tensor entries) Bogoliubov mode: This defines |vacA′⟩\ket{\mathrm{vac}_{A}^{\prime}} as the highest-weight bra Schmidt state of the same parity as the leading ket Schmidt state, which are expected to have a high overlap in our use cases. Furthermore, across all Schmidt vectors, this mode is expected to be excited the most often, so flipping it leads to the smallest possible increase in the size of the Pfaffians that need to be computed.

For left Schmidt vectors, the Bogoliubov mode operators are listed in order of increasing �\lambda, so the most entangled mode a0a_{0} appears closest to ⟨vacA|\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}} in the string of operators (20). Upon the particle-hole transformation, bra Schmidt states with or without an a0a_{0} Bogoliubov excitation transform as

⟨vacA|​a0​a�k​…​a�1\displaystyle\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{0}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}} =⟨vacA′|​a�k​…​a�1\displaystyle=\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}^{\prime}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}} (C.7a)
⟨vacA|​a�k​…​a�1\displaystyle\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}} =⟨vacA|​a0​a0†​a�k​…​a�1=⟨vacA′|​a0′​a�k​…​a�1,\displaystyle=\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{0}a_{0}^{\dagger}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}}=\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}^{\prime}}a^{\prime}_{0}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}}, (C.7b)

without generating any additional fermionic sign.

For right Schmidt vectors, the Bogoliubov mode operators are listed in order of decreasing �\lambda, so the most entangled mode a0a_{0} appears at the end of the string of a�a_{\alpha} in (20). Upon the particle-hole transformation, bra Schmidt states with or without an a0a_{0} Bogoliubov excitation transform as

⟨vacA|​a�k​…​a�1​a0\displaystyle\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}}a_{0} =(−1)k​⟨vacA|​a0​a�k​…​a�1=(−1)k​⟨vacA′|​a�k​…​a�1\displaystyle=(-1)^{k}\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{0}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}}=(-1)^{k}\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}^{\prime}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}} (C.8a)
⟨vacA|​a�k​…​a�1\displaystyle\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}} =⟨vacA|​a�k​…​a�1​a0​a0†=(−1)k​⟨vacA′|​a�k​…​a�1​a0′.\displaystyle=\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}}a_{0}a_{0}^{\dagger}=(-1)^{k}\bra{\mathrm{vac}_{A}^{\prime}}a_{\alpha_{k}}\dots a_{\alpha_{1}}a^{\prime}_{0}. (C.8b)

To account for this additional fermionic sign, we flip the sign of every bra Schmidt mode operator other than a0a_{0}.

Appendix E Practical implementation of the iMPS conversion

For finite bond dimensions, the Schmidt vectors |L�(L,n)⟩\ket{L_{\alpha}^{(L,n)}} and |L�(L−k,n)⟩\ket{L_{\alpha}^{(L-k,n)}} (or |R�(L,n+k)⟩\ket{R_{\beta}^{(L,n+k)}} and |R�(L−k,n)⟩\ket{R_{\beta}^{(L-k,n)}}) do not span the whole Hilbert space, so, generically, the overlap matrices (24) are not unitary. This means that instead of rotating the tensors at the ends of the iMPS unit cell using C0,D0C_{0},D_{0} directly, we have to find appropriate unitary rotations CC and DD.

Furthermore, for finite systems, the Schmidt values �\Lambda and �0\Lambda_{0} are not exactly equal for two different finite system sizes, adding an additional source of mismatch between the wave function | ⟩\ket{\Psi} on the longer chain, and its reconstruction | ~⟩\ket{\tilde{\Psi}} using the wave function on the shorter chain and the iMPS unit cell. In the following, we will find the unitary matrices CC and DD that maximise the overlap ⟨ ~| ⟩\braket{\tilde{\Psi}|\Psi} (Fig. 7).

For the sake of concreteness, we assume from here on that the iMPS unit cell is right canonical (this choice is built into TeMFpy as well). We will also assume that errors introduced by the iMPS construction on the left and right ends of the unit cell are independent, that is, when looking for the optimal CC, we assume that the optimal unitary DD is D0D_{0} and vice versa.

To find the optimal left gauge rotation matrix CC, we can thus contract down all the right canonical tensors in the right environment and the iMPS unit cell [Fig. 7(a)]. That is, the overlap of the two wave functions is given by tr⁡(�0​C0​�​C†)\tr(\Lambda_{0}C_{0}\Lambda C^{\dagger}), which can be maximised using the following result:

Lemma.

Let the singular value decomposition of a square matrix AA be A=U​�​V†A=U\Sigma V^{\dagger} and let all singular values be strictly positive. Then, the unitary matrix RR for which tr⁡(A​R†)\tr(AR^{\dagger}) is maximal is R=U​V†R=UV^{\dagger}.

Proof.

Let RR be a unitary matrix. Then tr⁡(A​R†)=tr⁡(U​�​V†​R†)=tr⁡(�​V†​R†​U)=∑i�i​(V†​R†​U)i​i\tr(AR^{\dagger})=\tr(U\Sigma V^{\dagger}R^{\dagger})=\tr(\Sigma V^{\dagger}R^{\dagger}U)=\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}(V^{\dagger}R^{\dagger}U)_{ii}. Since V†​R†​UV^{\dagger}R^{\dagger}U is unitary, its diagonal elements can be at most 1. Therefore, tr⁡(A​R†)\tr(AR^{\dagger}) is highest if all diagonal elements of V†​R†​UV^{\dagger}R^{\dagger}U are 1, i.e., if it is the identity matrix. Rearranging yields R=U​V†R=UV^{\dagger}. ∎

Finally, the smallest possible deviation between | ⟩\ket{\Psi} and | ~⟩\ket{\tilde{\Psi}} is

∥| ⟩−| ~⟩∥2\displaystyle\big\|\ket{\Psi}-\ket{\tilde{\Psi}}\big\|^{2} =tr⁡�2+tr⁡�02−tr⁡(C0​�​C†​�0)−tr⁡(�0​C​�​C0†)\displaystyle=\tr\Lambda^{2}+\tr\Lambda_{0}^{2}-\tr(C_{0}\Lambda C^{\dagger}\Lambda_{0})-\tr(\Lambda_{0}C\Lambda C_{0}^{\dagger})
=tr[(�0C−C0�)×H.c.]+tr[�(𝟙−C0†C0)�],\displaystyle=\tr\left[(\Lambda_{0}C-C_{0}\Lambda)\times\mathrm{H.c.}\right]+\tr\left[\Lambda(\mathbbm{1}-C_{0}^{\dagger}C_{0})\Lambda\right], (E.1)

where we used that CC is unitary. Both terms are nonnegative: the first is the Frobenius norm of �0​C−C0​�\Lambda_{0}C-C_{0}\Lambda; as for the second, diagonal entries of C0†​C0C_{0}^{\dagger}C_{0} are at most 1 (equal to 1 if C0C_{0} is unitary). In fact, we may assign distinct meanings to the two error terms:

  • •

    The second term measures the deviation of the overlap matrix C0C_{0} from being unitary, weighted with the corresponding Schmidt values. This error term can be reduced by keeping more Schmidt vectors, i.e., using higher bond dimensions.

  • •

    The first term, by contrast, measures the deviation of the Schmidt values �\Lambda and �0\Lambda_{0} and how accurately CC maps between them. This error term can be reduced by using larger system sizes, where finite-size differences between |L�(L,n)⟩\ket{L_{\alpha}^{(L,n)}} and |L�(L−k,n)⟩\ket{L_{\alpha}^{(L-k,n)}} are smaller.

Likewise, to find the optimal right gauge rotation matrix DD, we neglect the error introduced on the left hand side; in particular, we assume that C=C0C=C_{0} and �0​C=C​�\Lambda_{0}C=C\Lambda [first line of Fig. 7(b)]. Now, in order to contract down the left environment and the iMPS unit cell, we have to bring the latter to left canonical form by inserting the Schmidt values �−1\Lambda^{-1} and �~\tilde{\Lambda} on the left and right ends of the unit cell, respectively. In all, the overlap ⟨ ~| ⟩\braket{\tilde{\Psi}|\Psi} is reduced to tr⁡(�~2​D0​D†)\tr(\tilde{\Lambda}^{2}D_{0}D^{\dagger}), where �~\tilde{\Lambda} are the Schmidt values in the longer chain at the right end of the iMPS unit cell. The optimal DD follows from the same Lemma as above. The lowest possible deviation is given by

∥| ⟩−| ~⟩∥2\displaystyle\big\|\ket{\Psi}-\ket{\tilde{\Psi}}\big\|^{2} =tr⁡�~2+tr⁡�~2−tr⁡(�~​D0​D†​�~)−tr⁡(�~​D​D0†​�~)\displaystyle=\tr\tilde{\Lambda}^{2}+\tr\tilde{\Lambda}^{2}-\tr(\tilde{\Lambda}D_{0}D^{\dagger}\tilde{\Lambda})-\tr(\tilde{\Lambda}DD_{0}^{\dagger}\tilde{\Lambda})
=tr[(�~D−�~D0)×H.c.]+tr[�~(𝟙−D0D0†)�~].\displaystyle=\tr\left[(\tilde{\Lambda}D-\tilde{\Lambda}D_{0})\times\mathrm{H.c.}\right]+\tr\left[\tilde{\Lambda}(\mathbbm{1}-D_{0}D_{0}^{\dagger})\tilde{\Lambda}\right]. (E.2)

returns estimates of both error terms separately for both sides of the unit cell.
